prize_parts.citation: For the discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: IceCube is a clue from nature in the sense I care about. A cubic-kilometre detector in Antarctic ice found a flux of TeV-PeV neutrinos that no model had pinned down, and the existence of that flux is now confirmed through several independent analysis channels, with source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) following. It is both a discovery and a bold instrument, and it opens a new messenger for the extreme universe, which is exactly the kind of result the committee exists to recognise. Having read the other ballots, I note that B007 is ranked first by only two of us and ranks low or is absent for the others, so its support is narrow. I still think the narrow support reflects specialisation (Eva Olsson ranks it second, Goran Johansson and Eva Lindroth openly defer) rather than doubt about the science. The Halzen-Karle-Spiering trio is imperfect, but it is a workable allocation, and the leaders of the project are identifiable in a way they are not for the Higgs or the EHT.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. A collaboration of several hundred, plus the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND predecessors, means any three names will be contested, and Eva Olsson's own two-name version (Halzen and Karle) shows the committee has not converged on who the laureates are. Independent confirmation of the source populations by other detectors (KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD) is still partial. Meanwhile B015 is the only candidate ranked by all eight members and in the top five by every one of us, with a clean two-person attribution; if I am honest, it is the safer choice and I am advocating B007 partly on the discovery-first principle rather than on consensus. B015 is an invention and a precision advance in a field that already received prizes in 2005 and 2012, whereas B007 is a discovery of something new.

responses.point: Stefan ranks optical lattice clocks first because progress is limited by measurement precision, and he sees the lattice clock as a distinct step that prepares a redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with the science and ranked B015 second myself. Where I differ is on the weight of the argument that it is purely about precision. A clock at 1e-18 is a superb instrument, but the discovery content, for example in dark-matter couplings or constant drift, is still prospective, whereas IceCube already delivered a new observed phenomenon. The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 Wineland prize also does not seem to me fully answered by saying the step is distinct; I would like the committee to ask what nature told us here that we did not know. That said, I accept that the clean attribution to Katori and Ye is a real advantage over B007.

responses.point: Olle puts twisted bilayer graphene first as the clearest recent case of theory (the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat band) followed by decisive experiment, which opened moire quantum matter.
responses.response: The prediction followed by experiment is persuasive, and I put B006 third. My hesitation is maturity: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled, sample and twist-angle variability remains, and Olle himself lists these. A prize that sits at the start of a field that is still moving fast risks being revisited when the mechanism is understood. I also note that the experimental credit goes beyond the supplied names, since Yuan Cao is not on the list. I would not oppose B006, but I do not think it is more mature than IceCube, which is already established.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED first as a new regime of light-matter physics that became the architecture of superconducting processors, while flagging his own proximity to the field through WACQT.
responses.response: I appreciate the open flag on the conflict, and I agree that strong coupling on a chip is a real physical step. My reservation is timing: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is close enough that awarding the field again so soon would be hard to explain, as Stefan and Eva Olsson also suggest. The credited list also leaves out Girvin and Huang, which is a fairness question for a theory-plus-experiment story. Support for B024 is a single first place against two lower rankings, so I would treat it as a candidate for later years rather than this one.

responses.point: Eva argues that topological insulators (B055) extend the 2016 prize, because time-reversal-invariant topological insulators were not covered, and that the discovery is mature enough for recognition now.
responses.response: That is a fair distinction and it is why I keep B055 fourth rather than lower. I am not convinced it is as clean as she says: the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D work of Fu, Moore and Hasan sit outside the credited names, so the three-name prize would be historically incomplete, as Mark Pearce and Eva Olsson also note. It has strong support (four top-three placements) but no first place, which suggests it is a broadly acceptable second choice rather than something the committee is excited about.

responses.point: Eva ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a genuine invention that opened atom-by-atom imaging in materials and is overdue, and she notes her own possible field-proximity bias.
responses.response: I respect the maturity and impact argument and her candour about bias. My concern is that it is an enabling instrument whose impact lies in other fields, and the committee has to decide whether it counts as physics discovery; the omission of Krivanek and Dellby from the credited names, which Olle also raises, makes the attribution less clean than the three Rose-Haider-Urban names suggest. It is only ranked by three members, with two at rank six. I do note that she ranks IceCube second with a Halzen-Karle pair, which tells me we agree on the importance even if not on the trio.

responses.point: Mark ranks IceCube first as an instrument-led discovery that founded neutrino astronomy and bears on the origin of cosmic rays, while stating that source identification still needs time and that roles are uncertain.
responses.response: I agree, and I think Mark's point that source identification need not delay recognition of the discovery is the right way to frame it. Where I would push is on the third name: Mark, Eva Lindroth and I propose Spiering, Eva Olsson does not, so we should settle whether Spiering's role in AMANDA and the discovery analysis is decisive. I would also point out that Mark places B037 (Higgs experiments) third, which raises the same large-collaboration issue; if we are willing to accept three names for IceCube we should be consistent about it, but I find the attribution much more tractable for IceCube than for ATLAS and CMS.

uncertainties: Whether Karle, Spiering and Halzen are the right three, or whether Spiering should give way to someone else or the prize should have two names.
Whether the committee would accept source-population evidence from IceCube alone, or wants stronger independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD.
Whether B015 should be preferred because of its broad support and clean attribution, given the 2005 and 2012 overlap I raised.
My recollection of source-identification significance levels is from memory and has not been checked against external sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My research (string theory, dark energy, dark bubble cosmology) is distant from neutrino astronomy and atomic clocks, and I have no recorded personal or institutional tie to any of the credited names.
